w: נְשִׁיקַת פְּרֵדָה|a good-bye kiss|~lit. a kiss of parting
s.line: The next morning Dorothy kissed the pretty green girl good-bye,
s.note: בַּבֹּקֶר שֶׁלְּמָחֳרָת = "the next morning", from מָחָר (tomorrow); לְמָחֳרָת on its own = "on the following day". פְּרֵדָה = parting, a farewell. The verb is נִפְרַד מִ־ (to say good-bye to), which you will meet in sentence 10.

w: לָחֲצוּ יָד|shook hands|~idiom: pressed a hand
s.line: and they all shook hands with the soldier with the green whiskers, who had walked with them as far as the gate.
s.note: לָחַץ יָד לְ־ = to shake hands with someone (literally "to press a hand to"). לִוָּה (pi'el) = to go along with someone, to escort; מְלַוֶּה = a companion or escort. Do not confuse it with לָוָה (pa'al, to borrow money).

w: כְּשֶׁשּׁוֹמֵר הַשְּׁעָרִים|when the Guardian of the Gates
s.line: When the Guardian of the Gate saw them again he wondered greatly that they could leave the beautiful City to get into new trouble.
s.note: הִסְתַּבֵּךְ = to get tangled up, to get into trouble. It is hitpa'el, and the ת of the prefix swaps places with the first root letter ס. The same root gives סָבוּךְ (tangled, complicated) and סִבּוּךְ (a complication). הִתְפַּלֵּא = to be amazed, from פֶּלֶא (a wonder).

s.line: But he at once unlocked their spectacles, which he put back into the green box,
s.note: הֶחֱזִיר (hif'il) = to give back, to put back; pa'al חָזַר = to come back. The hif'il often means "to make someone or something do" the pa'al action: הֶחֱזִיר = "made (it) go back". In a shop: אֶפְשָׁר לְהַחֲזִיר אֶת זֶה? (can I return this?).

s.line: and gave them many good wishes to carry with them.
s.note: אִחֵל (to wish) and אִחוּלִים (wishes) share a root, a verb + noun pair like the ones you already know. On a birthday card: אִחוּלִים לְיוֹם הֻלֶּדֶת. לַדֶּרֶךְ = "for the road / for the journey": אֹכֶל לַדֶּרֶךְ (food for the trip).

s.line: “You are now our ruler,” he said to the Scarecrow;

w: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר|as soon as possible|~idiom: as much more quickly as can be
s.line: “so you must come back to us as soon as possible.”
s.note: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר מַהֵר is the everyday "as soon as possible", the Hebrew ASAP. The pattern works with other words too: כְּמָה שֶׁיּוֹתֵר זוֹל (as cheap as possible). A more formal version is בְּהֶקְדֵּם הָאֶפְשָׁרִי, which you will see in letters and emails.

w: שֶׁאֶחֱזֹר|that I will come back|pa'al · ח־ז־ר
s.line: “I certainly shall if I am able,” the Scarecrow replied;
“but I must help Dorothy to get home, first.”
s.note: עָזַר לְ־: in Hebrew you help to someone, so it is לַעֲזֹר לְדוֹרוֹתִי, never אֶת. אוּכַל is the future of יָכֹל ("I will be able"), a form worth memorizing: אוּכַל, תּוּכַל, יוּכַל.

s.line: As Dorothy bade the good-natured Guardian a last farewell she said:
s.note: נִפְרַד מִ־ = to part from, to say good-bye to. It is nif'al with an active meaning, so no underline. It is also used for couples: הֵם נִפְרְדוּ (they broke up). טוֹב לֵב = kind-hearted, an adjective made like a construct pair; with the article, the הַ goes on the second word: הַשּׁוֹמֵר טוֹב הַלֵּב.

s.line: “I have been very kindly treated in your lovely City, and everyone has been good to me.
s.note: הִתְיַחֵס אֶל / לְ־ = to treat (someone), and also "to relate to, to refer to": הוּא לֹא הִתְיַחֵס לַשְּׁאֵלָה (he didn't address the question). Here the plural verb with no subject replaces the English passive "I have been treated", as in chapter 1.

w: אֲסִירַת תּוֹדָה|grateful (fem.)|~idiom: a prisoner of thanks
s.line: I cannot tell you how grateful I am.”
s.note: אָסִיר תּוֹדָה (fem. אֲסִירַת תּוֹדָה) = "grateful", literally "a prisoner of thanks". It is a little formal but very common in speeches and letters: אֲנִי אֲסִיר תּוֹדָה עַל הָעֶזְרָה. לְתָאֵר = to describe; תֵּאוּר = a description, תֹּאַר = an adjective (and also a degree, as in תֹּאַר רִאשׁוֹן, a B.A.).

s.line: “Don’t try, my dear,” he answered.
s.note: "Don't!" is אַל + the future: אַל תְּנַסִּי, אַל תִּדְאַג (don't worry). For a general rule or a sign, Hebrew uses לֹא + infinitive: לֹא לְעַשֵּׁן (no smoking).

w: הָיִינוּ רוֹצִים|we would like|~conditional: we were wanting
s.line: “We should like to keep you with us, but if it is your wish to return to Kansas, I hope you will find a way.”
s.note: הָיִינוּ רוֹצִים = "we would like": past of הָיָה + participle makes the conditional, the polite form you hear in shops: הָיִיתִי רוֹצֶה קָפֶה (I'd like a coffee). לְהַשְׁאִיר (hif'il, to leave behind, to keep) pairs with nif'al נִשְׁאַר (to stay, remain).

w: יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out on their journey|~idiom: went out to the road
s.line: He then opened the gate of the outer wall, and they walked forth and started upon their journey.
s.note: יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = to set out, literally "to go out to the road". It is also used of projects: הַפְּרוֹיֶקְט יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ (the project got under way).

s.line: The sun shone brightly as our friends turned their faces toward the Land of the South.
s.note: שֶׁמֶשׁ is feminine here, hence זָרְחָה. הִפְנָה (hif'il, to turn something toward) and פָּנָה (pa'al, to turn, to approach) share their letters with פָּנִים (face). הִפְנָה is also "to refer": הָרוֹפֵא הִפְנָה אוֹתִי לְמֻמְחֶה (the doctor referred me to a specialist).

w: בְּמַצַּב רוּחַ|in a mood|~lit. state of spirit
s.line: They were all in the best of spirits, and laughed and chatted together.
s.note: מַצַּב רוּחַ = mood: יֵשׁ לִי מַצַּב רוּחַ טוֹב (I'm in a good mood). מְצֻיָּן (excellent) is in form a pu'al participle, like מְאֻשָּׁר: "marked out, distinguished". פִּטְפֵּט = to chatter, a pi'el with a four-letter root, which you will also hear for a chatterbox: פַּטְפְּטָן.

s.line: Dorothy was once more filled with the hope of getting home,
and the Scarecrow and the Tin Woodman were glad to be of use to her.
s.note: הִתְמַלֵּא (hitpa'el) = to fill up, to become full, from מָלֵא (full). לִהְיוֹת לְעֵזֶר לְ־ = to be of help to someone; at the end of a call you might hear שָׂמַחְתִּי לַעֲזֹר (glad to help).

w: וּבַאֲשֶׁר לָאַרְיֵה|as for the Lion|~set phrase: as regards
עַל כָּךְ שֶׁ|at the fact that|~fixed phrase
s.line: As for the Lion, he sniffed the fresh air with delight and whisked his tail from side to side in pure joy at being in the country again,
s.note: בַּאֲשֶׁר לְ־ = "as for, regarding", a higher-register phrase you will read in the news: בַּאֲשֶׁר לַתַּקְצִיב… (as for the budget…). מֵרֹב + noun = "from so much …": מֵרֹב עֲיֵפוּת (out of sheer tiredness). הֵנִיף = to wave or swing; הֵנִיף דֶּגֶל = to wave a flag.

s.line: while Toto ran around them and chased the moths and butterflies, barking merrily all the time.
s.note: רָדַף אַחֲרֵי = to chase after. The same verb is used for persecution: רְדִיפָה. פַּרְפַּר לַיְלָה ("night butterfly") is the everyday word for a moth.

s.line: “City life does not agree with me at all,” remarked the Lion, as they walked along at a brisk pace.
s.note: חַיִּים (life) is always plural in Hebrew, so the verb is plural too: הַחַיִּים … לֹא מַתְאִימִים. זֶה לֹא מַתְאִים לִי = "it doesn't suit me", and also "that's not like me". קֶצֶב = pace, and also rhythm in music.

w: יָרַדְתִּי בַּמִּשְׁקָל|I have lost weight|~idiom: I went down in weight
s.line: “I have lost much flesh since I lived there,
s.note: יָרַד בַּמִּשְׁקָל = to lose weight; the opposite is עָלָה בַּמִּשְׁקָל. Prices go the same way: הַמְּחִירִים עָלוּ (prices went up). מֵאָז שֶׁ = "since" (in time): מֵאָז שֶׁעָבַרְנוּ לְכָאן (since we moved here).

w: בְּקֹצֶר רוּחַ|impatiently|~idiom: with shortness of spirit
s.line: and now I am anxious for a chance to show the other beasts how courageous I have grown.”
s.note: בְּקֹצֶר רוּחַ = impatiently, literally "with shortness of spirit"; אֲנִי מְחַכֶּה בְּקֹצֶר רוּחַ is the usual "I can't wait". הִזְדַּמְּנוּת (a chance, an opportunity) is a hitpa'el noun: the ת of the prefix becomes ד after ז. נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) here means "became", not "was done".

w: וְהֵעִיפוּ מַבָּט|and took a look|~idiom: made a look fly
s.line: They now turned and took a last look at the Emerald City.
s.note: הֵעִיף מַבָּט בְּ־ = to glance at, literally "to make a look fly at"; הֵעִיף on its own = to throw out, to make fly (הֵעִיפוּ אוֹתוֹ מֵהָעֲבוֹדָה, slang for "he got fired"). הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn around, to go around; לְהִסְתּוֹבֵב בָּעִיר = to wander around town.

s.line: All they could see was a mass of towers and steeples behind the green walls,
s.note: צְרִיחַ = a turret or steeple, and also the rook in chess. הָמוֹן = a crowd or a mass; in speech it is the common word for "lots of": יֵשׁ לִי הָמוֹן עֲבוֹדָה.

s.line: and high up above everything the spires and dome of the Palace of Oz.
s.note: מְחֻדָּד = sharpened, pointed: the pu'al participle of חִדֵּד (to sharpen), from חַד (sharp). כִּפָּה = a dome, and also the skullcap (kippah); same word, same shape.

w: בְּסַךְ הַכֹּל|after all|~idiom: in the sum of everything
s.line: “Oz was not such a bad Wizard, after all,” said the Tin Woodman, as he felt his heart rattling around in his breast.
s.note: בְּסַךְ הַכֹּל = "all in all, after all", and also "only, merely": הוּא בְּסַךְ הַכֹּל יֶלֶד (he's only a kid). קִשְׁקֵשׁ = to rattle, and in everyday speech also to talk nonsense or to scribble; קִשְׁקוּשִׁים! = "nonsense!".

s.line: “He knew how to give me brains, and very good brains, too,” said the Scarecrow.
s.note: יָדַע + infinitive = "knew how to": אֲנִי יוֹדֵעַ לִשְׂחוֹת (I can swim). וְעוֹד + noun = "and a … at that": הוּא קָנָה מְכוֹנִית, וְעוֹד חֲדָשָׁה (he bought a car, and a new one at that).

s.line: “If Oz had taken a dose of the same courage he gave me,” added the Lion, “he would have been a brave man.”
s.note: אִלּוּ introduces an unreal condition ("if he had …, he would have …"). Both halves use הָיָה + participle, or simply הָיָה: אִלּוּ יָדַעְתִּי, הָיִיתִי בָּא (had I known, I would have come). In speech you will often hear אִם used the same way. מָנָה = a dose, and also a portion or a course at a meal: מָנָה רִאשׁוֹנָה (a first course).

s.line: Dorothy said nothing.

w: כְּמֵיטַב יְכָלְתּוֹ|his best|~idiom: according to the best of his ability
s.line: Oz had not kept the promise he made her, but he had done his best, so she forgave him.
s.note: קִיֵּם הַבְטָחָה = to keep a promise (pi'el of the root of קָם, "to make it stand"). You give a promise: נָתַן הַבְטָחָה. סָלַח לְ־ = to forgive someone; its noun is the everyday סְלִיחָה (sorry / excuse me). כְּמֵיטַב יְכָלְתּוֹ = "to the best of his ability", a fixed phrase.

s.line: As he said, he was a good man, even if he was a bad Wizard.
The first day’s journey was through the green fields and bright flowers that stretched about the Emerald City on every side.
s.note: הִשְׂתָּרֵעַ = to stretch out, to extend over an area, a hitpa'el where the ת swaps with שׂ. You'll read it in geography and the news: הַשֶּׁטַח מִשְׂתָּרֵעַ עַל אֶלֶף דּוּנָם (the area extends over a thousand dunams). דֶּרֶךְ is usually feminine, hence עָבְרָה.

s.line: They slept that night on the grass, with nothing but the stars over them;
and they rested very well indeed.
s.note: נָח (to rest) is a hollow verb: the root's middle ו disappears in the past (נָחוּ), but returns in מְנוּחָה (rest). The hif'il הֵנִיחַ = to put down, to lay (and also to assume).

s.line: In the morning they traveled on until they came to a thick wood.
s.note: סָבוּךְ = tangled, dense; also "complicated": מַצָּב סָבוּךְ. It is the same root as לְהִסְתַּבֵּךְ in sentence 3. הִמְשִׁיךְ = to continue (hif'il of the root of מָשַׁךְ); תַּמְשִׁיךְ! = "go on!".

s.line: There was no way of going around it, for it seemed to extend to the right and left as far as they could see;
s.note: עָקַף = to go around, to bypass, and in driving, to overtake: אָסוּר לַעֲקֹף (no overtaking). A כְּבִישׁ עוֹקֵף is a bypass road. The ה in יָמִינָה and שְׂמֹאלָה means "toward", as in הַבַּיְתָה.

w: שֶׁיֵּלְכוּ לְאִבּוּד|that they would get lost|~idiom: would go to loss
s.line: and, besides, they did not dare change the direction of their journey for fear of getting lost.
s.note: הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = to get lost, literally "to go to loss"; things go missing the same way: הַמִּזְוָדָה הָלְכָה לְאִבּוּד (the suitcase got lost). הֵעֵז = to dare; אַל תָּעֵז! = "don't you dare!".

s.line: So they looked for the place where it would be easiest to get into the forest.
The Scarecrow, who was in the lead, finally discovered a big tree with such wide-spreading branches that there was room for the party to pass underneath.
s.note: בָּרֹאשׁ = "at the head, in the lead": הַקְּבוּצָה בָּרֹאשׁ (the team is on top). הִתְפַּשֵּׁט = to spread (a fire, a disease, an idea), and also, more often in daily life, to get undressed. שֶׁהָעֲנָפִים שֶׁלּוֹ ("that its branches") is how modern Hebrew says "whose".

s.line: So he walked forward to the tree, but just as he came under the first branches they bent down and twined around him,

w: עִם הָרֹאשׁ קָדִימָה|headlong|~lit. with the head forward
s.line: and the next minute he was raised from the ground and flung headlong among his fellow travelers.
s.note: Two hof'al passives, each with its active hif'il: הֵרִים (lifted) → הוּרַם (was lifted), and הִשְׁלִיךְ (threw away) → הֻשְׁלַךְ (was thrown). The hof'al has a וּ or ֻ after the first letter.

s.line: This did not hurt the Scarecrow, but it surprised him, and he looked rather dizzy when Dorothy picked him up.
s.note: הִכְאִיב לְ־ (hif'il) = to cause pain to someone; the pa'al כָּאַב = to ache: כּוֹאֵב לִי הָרֹאשׁ (I have a headache). מְסֻחְרָר = dizzy, a pu'al participle of a four-letter root; סְחַרְחֹרֶת = dizziness, and סְחַרְחֵרָה = a merry-go-round.

s.line: “Here is another space between the trees,” called the Lion.
s.note: רֶוַח = a gap or space (also the space between words), and also profit: רְוָחִים (profits) in the business news.

s.line: “Let me try it first,” said the Scarecrow, “for it doesn’t hurt me to get thrown about.”
s.note: תֵּן לִי / תְּנוּ לִי + infinitive = "let me …": תֵּן לִי לַחְשֹׁב (let me think). כְּשֶׁזּוֹרְקִים אוֹתִי = "when I get thrown": again a plural participle with no subject in place of an English passive.

w: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי דִּבּוּר|as he spoke|~idiom: in the course of speech
s.line: He walked up to another tree, as he spoke, but its branches immediately seized him and tossed him back again.
s.note: תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי + noun = "while doing": תּוֹךְ כְּדֵי נְסִיעָה (while driving). נִגַּשׁ לְ־ = to go up to, to approach, nif'al with an active meaning; it also means to take an exam: נִגַּשְׁתִּי לַבְּחִינָה.

s.line: “This is strange,” exclaimed Dorothy.
“What shall we do?”
s.note: Without vowels, נעשה can be read two ways: נַעֲשֶׂה (pa'al future, "we will do") or נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al past, "was done" or "became", as in נַעֲשֵׂיתִי in sentence 24). מָה נַעֲשֶׂה? is the everyday "what shall we do?".

s.line: “The trees seem to have made up their minds to fight us, and stop our journey,” remarked the Lion.
s.note: נִלְחַם בְּ־ = to fight against: nif'al with an active meaning, and it takes בְּ־, not אֶת. The pa'al participle לוֹחֵם = a fighter or combat soldier, which gives the chapter's הָעֵצִים הַלּוֹחֲמִים. נִרְאֶה שֶׁ… = "it seems that …".

s.line: “I believe I will try it myself,” said the Woodman,
and shouldering his axe, he marched up to the first tree that had handled the Scarecrow so roughly.
s.note: טִפֵּל בְּ־ = to handle, to deal with, to take care of: אֲנִי אֲטַפֵּל בָּזֶה (I'll take care of it). The noun טִפּוּל is "treatment" or "therapy", and a מְטַפֶּלֶת is a therapist or a nanny. בְּגַסּוּת = roughly, rudely, from גַּס (coarse, rude).

s.line: When a big branch bent down to seize him the Woodman chopped at it so fiercely that he cut it in two.
s.note: הִכָּה (to hit) is the hif'il of a root starting with נ, which drops out and leaves a dagesh in the כּ. The noun is מַכָּה (a blow). לִשְׁנַיִם = "in two": לַחְתֹּךְ לִשְׁנַיִם.

s.line: At once the tree began shaking all its branches as if in pain, and the Tin Woodman passed safely under it.
s.note: בְּשָׁלוֹם = safely, unharmed: הִגַּעְנוּ הַבַּיְתָה בְּשָׁלוֹם (we got home safely). כְּאִלּוּ = "as if", and in casual speech a filler like English "like": הוּא, כְּאִלּוּ, לֹא הֵבִין.

s.line: “Come on!” he shouted to the others.
“Be quick!”
They all ran forward and passed under the tree without injury, except Toto, who was caught by a small branch and shaken until he howled.
s.note: Two passives: נִתְפַּס (nif'al of תָּפַס, to catch) = was caught, and טֻלְטַל (pu'al of טִלְטֵל, to shake about) = was shaken. עַל יְדֵי = "by" (the doer of a passive). טִלְטוּלִים is what you feel on a bumpy bus ride. פֶּגַע = harm, injury; נִפְגַּע = was hurt.

s.line: But the Woodman promptly chopped off the branch and set the little dog free.
s.note: שִׁחְרֵר = to set free, to release; שִׁחְרוּר = release, liberation, and in Israel also discharge from the army: הוּא הִשְׁתַּחְרֵר מֵהַצָּבָא. כָּרַת = to cut down or cut off (trees, limbs); כְּרִיתָה = felling.

s.line: The other trees of the forest did nothing to keep them back,
s.note: עִכֵּב = to hold up, to delay; עִכּוּב = a delay: יֵשׁ עִכּוּב בַּטִּיסָה (the flight is delayed). The nif'al נִשְׁאַר you know; שְׁאָר = "the rest of", from the same root.

s.line: so they made up their minds that only the first row of trees could bend down their branches,
s.note: הִסִּיק = to conclude, to infer, mostly in הִסִּיק מַסְקָנוֹת (to draw conclusions); מַסְקָנָה is from the same root. Its נ drops out like הִכָּה in sentence 53. הִטָּה = to bend, to tilt; in grammar, נְטִיָּה is an inflection.

w: שֶׁקִּבְּלוּ|who had been given|~lit. who received
s.line: and that probably these were the policemen of the forest, and given this wonderful power in order to keep strangers out of it.
s.note: כַּנִּרְאֶה = apparently, probably ("as is seen"), very common in the news. מָנַע מִ־ X לְ־ + infinitive = to prevent X from doing: הַגֶּשֶׁם מָנַע מֵאִתָּנוּ לָצֵאת (the rain kept us from going out). Here קִבְּלוּ ("received") replaces the English passive "were given".

s.line: The four travelers walked with ease through the trees until they came to the farther edge of the wood.
s.note: אַרְבַּעַת הַנּוֹסְעִים = "the four travelers": with a definite noun the number takes its construct form (אַרְבָּעָה → אַרְבַּעַת), as in שְׁלֹשֶׁת הַיְּלָדִים. בְּקַלּוּת = easily, from קַל.

s.line: Then, to their surprise, they found before them a high wall which seemed to be made of white china.
s.note: עָשׂוּי מִ־ = made of: הַשֻּׁלְחָן עָשׂוּי מֵעֵץ. חַרְסִינָה = china, porcelain; Israelis also use it for glazed ceramic tiles. לְהַפְתָּעָתָם = "to their surprise", one of the fixed forms with a possessive ending (לְהַפְתָּעָתִי, to my surprise).

s.line: It was smooth, like the surface of a dish, and higher than their heads.
s.note: גְּבוֹהָה מֵ־ = higher than: Hebrew can make a comparison with מִן alone, without יוֹתֵר. חָלָק (smooth) and חֵלֶק (a part) look the same without vowels: חלק. פְּנֵי = the face of, here "the surface of"; פְּנֵי הַיָּם = sea level.

s.line: “What shall we do now?” asked Dorothy.
“I will make a ladder,” said the Tin Woodman, “for we certainly must climb over the wall.”
s.note: טִפֵּס = to climb; מְטַפֵּס = a climber, קִיר טִפּוּס = a climbing wall. בָּרוּר = clear, obvious; בָּרוּר! on its own is a common "of course!".
